title: Web services: probes, jobs, config and request pipeline
description: Liveness versus readiness, scheduled and background jobs on several instances, retries and backoff arithmetic, secrets and layered config, middleware ordering and blocking versus non-blocking I/O.
source: Kubernetes probe documentation; the twelve-factor app (config); Redis SET documentation; cron(5) manual; Google SRE book (retries and backoff); server-sent events section of the HTML Living Standard
seriesTitle: Core: HTTP, API and data-access concepts
seriesDescription: Status codes, pagination, idempotency, probes, secrets, pool arithmetic, isolation and N+1 as SQL. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.

questions.prompt: A service depends on a database. Where should the database check live to avoid a restart storm during a database outage?

options.text: In the liveness check, so that pods which cannot reach the database are restarted as quickly as possible.
options.why: A database outage would restart every instance and prolong recovery.

options.text: In both checks with identical timeouts, for symmetry.
options.why: This still restarts healthy processes whenever the dependency blips.

options.text: In the readiness check only; liveness should reflect only that the process itself is healthy.
options.why: Correct: failing readiness stops traffic without killing healthy processes.

options.text: In neither; health checks must never touch dependencies.
options.why: Readiness checks on critical dependencies are standard practice.

questions.explanation: Liveness answers "should this process be killed?"; readiness answers "should it receive traffic right now?". Keep both cheap and time-boxed.

questions.prompt: Match each Kubernetes probe or component with what it does.

right.text: The pod is removed from Service endpoints but is not restarted
Other probes wait until a slow boot has finished
Adds or removes replicas based on a metric such as CPU

questions.explanation: Startup probes protect slow-starting containers from being killed by the liveness probe. Autoscaling is a separate control loop and never restarts a container.

questions.prompt: A Unix cron entry reads `"30 2 * * 1-5"` (minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week, with `1-5` meaning Monday to Friday). How many times does it fire in one seven-day week?
questions.explanation: It fires at `02:30` on each of the five weekdays: 5 runs. Unix cron has five fields; some schedulers add a leading seconds field, so always check the dialect.

questions.prompt: A job loop waits 2 seconds after each run finishes before starting the next run (fixed delay). Each run takes 3 seconds and the first run starts at `t = 0 s` on a single thread. How many runs have started by `t = 62 s`, counting the one at `t = 0`?
questions.explanation: Each cycle is `3 + 2 = 5 s`, so runs start at 0, 5, 10 ... 60: that is 13 starts. A fixed-rate schedule on one thread would instead start the next run as soon as a late one ends, never overlapping.

questions.prompt: An application has a nightly cleanup job triggered by an in-process scheduler. It is deployed as 3 identical replicas and nothing coordinates them. How many times does the cleanup run each night across the cluster?
questions.explanation: Every replica has its own scheduler, so the job runs 3 times. Fixes: a distributed lock, leader election, a dedicated scheduler instance, or a cluster-level cron job that triggers one run.

questions.prompt: Write the single Redis command that sets key `lock:nightly` to the value `1` only if the key does not exist, expiring after 300 seconds, so that only one instance runs the job.
questions.explanation: `SET` with `NX` and `EX` is one atomic step, unlike `SETNX` followed by `EXPIRE` (a crash between them leaves a lock that never expires). The reply is `OK` for the winner and `nil` for everyone else. Choose a TTL longer than the job, or renew it.

questions.prompt: A call is wrapped in a retry policy of "the first attempt plus 3 retries" and the operation always fails. How many times is it executed in total?
questions.explanation: 1 first attempt + 3 retries = 4 executions. Always check whether a library counts "attempts" (total) or "retries" (extra), because the two readings differ by one.

questions.prompt: A client retries with exponential backoff: it waits 1 s before the first retry, then doubles the wait each time, and makes 4 retries in total (all fail). How many seconds does it spend waiting overall, ignoring the time the calls themselves take?
questions.explanation: Waits are 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15 s. Add random jitter and a cap in practice so many clients do not retry in lockstep.

questions.prompt: Judge the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: Handlers of a job queue should be written to be idempotent.
questions.reason: Message queues with acknowledgements guarantee exactly-once execution by default.

whys.c: Correct: A is true and R is false; delivery is typically at-least-once, so a crash or visibility timeout can run a job twice.

questions.explanation: Make handlers safe to repeat with idempotency keys, upserts or "already processed" markers.

questions.prompt: Judge the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: Work that a web process continues after sending its response can be lost if that process crashes.
questions.reason: The pending work is held only in the memory of that process.

whys.a: Correct: nothing durable records the unfinished work, so a crash silently drops it.
whys.b: Wrong: R is exactly the mechanism.

questions.explanation: Fine for best-effort work such as a welcome e-mail; use a durable queue or an outbox table when the work must happen.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which are sound practices for configuration and secrets?

options.text: Inject passwords through environment variables or a secrets manager.
options.why: Keeps secrets out of the repository and out of the image.

options.text: Commit the production configuration file with the real database password.
options.why: Anything in version-control history must be treated as compromised.

options.text: Validate required configuration at startup so a missing value fails fast.
options.why: A crash at boot is cheaper than a failure on the first request.

options.text: Log all settings at startup to help debugging.
options.why: That writes secrets into log aggregation.

options.text: Mask secret values in logs, diagnostics pages and error reports.
options.why: Log aggregation systems are widely readable and long-lived.

options.text: Bake the API key into the container image.
options.why: Anyone who can pull the image can read the key.

questions.explanation: Principle: config in the environment (twelve-factor), secrets from a vault, validate at boot, never log them, rotate them.

questions.prompt: The same setting appears in a file packaged with the application, in an environment variable, and in a command-line flag. Under the usual layered-configuration convention, which value wins?

options.text: The packaged file, because it was reviewed and committed.
options.why: Packaged defaults are the lowest layer so operators can override them without a rebuild.

options.text: Whichever source was read first, because later ones are ignored.
options.why: Layered configuration merges sources and lets later, higher-priority ones override.

options.text: The environment variable, but only when the flag is absent and the file is empty.
options.why: The file being empty has no bearing on the order; priority is fixed.

options.text: The command-line flag, then the environment variable, then the packaged file.
options.why: Correct: more specific and more external sources override more general, packaged ones.

questions.explanation: Rule of thumb: external beats packaged, specific beats general. Document the order in your service so operators are not surprised.

questions.prompt: A request pipeline wraps the handler in four layers numbered 1 (outermost) to 4 (innermost). A request passes through layers 1, 2, 3, 4, then the handler, and the response travels back out through the same layers in reverse. At which position (1 = first) does layer 2 see the response?
questions.explanation: The response unwinds 4, 3, 2, 1, so layer 2 is third. Keep this onion shape in mind when ordering authentication, logging and compression layers.

questions.prompt: Judge the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: An object shared by all request-handling threads is automatically thread-safe.
questions.reason: A shared object means every thread can read and write the same fields.

whys.c: Wrong: A is false; R is true.
whys.d: Correct: sharing is exactly why unsynchronised mutable state is dangerous. Keep shared objects stateless or guard the state.

questions.explanation: Shared means shared, not synchronised: prefer immutable or stateless components, or use locks and atomic types.

questions.prompt: A server handles requests on a single-threaded event loop. Each handler makes a blocking call that takes 2 seconds without yielding to the loop, and 3 requests arrive at the same instant. About how many seconds until the last response is sent?
questions.explanation: A blocking call freezes the loop, so handlers run one after another: 3 x 2 = 6 s. With a non-blocking wait of 2 s each, the three would overlap and finish in about 2 s.

questions.prompt: Blocking handlers run on a pool of 40 worker threads. Each handler sleeps for 1 second, and 100 requests arrive at the same instant. About how many seconds until the last response?
questions.explanation: Requests run in batches of 40, 40 and 20, so three rounds of 1 s: about 3 s. Raising the pool size or going non-blocking changes this arithmetic.

questions.text: An SSE response uses the media type {1}; each event is one or more lines starting with {2} and is terminated by {3}.
questions.explanation: The browser `EventSource` reconnects automatically and sends `Last-Event-ID` if the server set `id:` lines. Remember that proxies must not buffer the response.

questions.prompt: Write the container probe section of a Kubernetes pod spec: a `livenessProbe` doing an HTTP GET on `/live` and a `readinessProbe` doing an HTTP GET on `/ready`, both on port `8080`.
questions.model:
livenessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /live
    port: 8080
readinessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /ready
    port: 8080
questions.explanation: Real manifests also set `initialDelaySeconds`, `periodSeconds` and `failureThreshold`; a `startupProbe` is added for slow boots. The endpoint behind `/live` must not call the database.
